newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. wheat prospects rosy in 1998 - USDA economist.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wheat prospects rosy in 1998 - USDA economist.

text.p: The prospects for U.S. wheat sales in 1998 look rosy because of an expected fall in output in Argentina and Australia, a senior U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) economist said on Thursday.

"With the uncertainty regarding southern hemisphere crops this year in both Argentina and Australia, we know there'll be less wheat from those markets," the USDA official told Reuters in an interview at a wheat conference in Singapore.
"We're going to have more wheat this year from our own crop," he said.

Argentina and Australia have emerged as rivals to U.S. wheat farmers after harvesting record crops in the 1996/97 season. Australia reaped a record 24 million tonnes while Argentina harvested 16 million tonnes of wheat.
The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) this month pegged the wheat crop at 15-16 million tonnes, down from its original estimate of 18 million.
The prospect of the El Nino weather anomaly triggering drought in Australia prompted the AWB to trim the forecast.
In Argentina, the government's Agricultural Secretariat has said wheat sowings for 1997/98 are down nearly 15 percent to an estimated 6.25 million hectares (15.4 million acres).
Traders estimated Argentina's wheat crop will probably range betwen 12.5 to 14 million tonnes.
The USDA, on the other hand, said in its July report that it expected the winter wheat harvest to climb 20 percent from a year ago to reach 1.78 billion bushels.
